items.prompt: How do we see a book on a table in a lit room?

options.text: Light from a lamp or the Sun reflects off the book into our eyes.
Light comes out of our eyes and hits the book.
options.why: Our eyes do not give out light. About 1,000 years ago, Ibn al-Haytham showed that light enters the eye.

options.text: The book gives out its own light.
options.why: A book is not a light source. It only reflects light.

options.text: Our eyes can see without any light.
options.why: With no light at all, we cannot see anything.

hints: A book is not a light source.
Light must travel from a source to the book, then on to somewhere else.
Trace the light from the lamp to the book. Then decide where it goes next.
items.explanation: Light from a source hits the book and reflects off it. Some of the reflected light enters our eyes, so we see the book.

items.prompt: Sort these surfaces into ones that give a clear reflection and ones that do not.
hints: A clear reflection needs a very smooth, shiny surface.
Rough surfaces scatter light in every direction.
Start with the mirror, then think about a pond on a calm day.
items.explanation: Smooth, shiny surfaces such as mirrors, still water and polished metal reflect light neatly and give clear images. Rough or dark surfaces scatter or absorb light, so they give no clear reflection.

items.prompt: A ray of light hits a flat mirror. The angle of incidence is 35°. What is the angle of reflection?
hints: Both angles are measured from the normal, a line at right angles to the mirror.
For a flat mirror, the two angles follow a simple rule.
Ask how the angle of reflection compares with the angle of incidence.
items.explanation: The angle of reflection always equals the angle of incidence. So the reflected ray leaves at 35° to the normal.

items.prompt: Why is the word AMBULANCE often written backwards on the front of an ambulance?

options.text: Because ambulances drive backwards.
options.why: Ambulances drive forwards. The word is reversed for people looking in mirrors.

options.text: To make it look more interesting.
options.why: The reason is practical: mirrors flip the word.

options.text: Because it is written in another language.
options.why: It is the same English word, just reversed.

options.text: So drivers ahead can read it the right way round in their mirrors.

hints: Think about how drivers see the vehicles behind them.
A mirror image is reversed from left to right.
Ask what happens to backwards writing when it is seen in a mirror.
items.explanation: A mirror reverses an image from left to right. Writing the word backwards means drivers see it the right way round in their rear-view mirrors.

items.prompt: A straw in a glass of water looks bent at the water's surface. Why?

options.text: The water bends the straw.
options.why: Take the straw out and it is still straight. Only the light changes direction.

options.text: Light changes direction as it passes from water into air.
Light travels in curves through water.
options.why: Light travels in straight lines inside the water. It changes direction at the surface.

options.text: The glass acts like a mirror.
options.why: The effect comes from light passing through the water's surface, not from a reflection.

hints: The straw is not really bent. Something happens to the light.
Light changes speed when it moves from one transparent material into another.
Look at where the straw seems to bend: exactly at the surface of the water.
items.explanation: Light from the straw changes direction as it leaves the water and enters the air. This bending of light is called refraction, and it makes the straw look bent.

items.prompt: Put these steps in order to explain how you see a flower in sunlight.
items: your eye sends a signal to your brain
hints: Start at the light source.
The flower does not make light. It reflects it.
The last step happens inside your head.
items.explanation: Light travels from the Sun to the flower and reflects off it. The reflected light enters your eye, and nerves carry a signal to your brain.

items.prompt: Why does a swimming pool look shallower than it really is?

options.text: The water magnifies the tiles and brings them closer.
options.why: The effect comes from light changing direction at the surface, not from magnifying.

options.text: The pool floor rises during the day.
options.why: The floor does not move. Only the light changes direction.

options.text: Light from the bottom refracts as it leaves the water, so the bottom seems higher.
Water absorbs the light from the deep parts.
options.why: Some light is absorbed, but that does not make the pool look shallower.

hints: This is another effect of light bending at the surface of water.
Your brain assumes that light always travels in straight lines.
Trace light from the bottom of the pool to your eye, bending at the surface.
items.explanation: Light from the bottom bends as it leaves the water. Your brain traces the light back in a straight line, so the bottom seems higher than it really is.
items.tip: Always check the depth sign before you jump into a pool.

items.prompt: Draw a ray of light hitting a flat mirror and reflecting off it. Draw the normal, and label the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection.

criteria.label: Draws straight rays with arrows showing the direction of light
Draws the normal at 90° to the mirror
Makes the angle of reflection equal to the angle of incidence

hints: Use a ruler and a protractor.
Measure both angles from the normal, not from the mirror.
items.explanation: The normal is a line at 90° to the mirror where the ray hits it. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and both are measured from the normal.

items.prompt: In 1666, Isaac Newton passed sunlight through a glass prism and saw a band of colours. What did this show?

options.text: The prism adds colour to the light.
options.why: Newton used a second prism to join the colours back into white light, so the colours were already in sunlight.

options.text: White light is a mixture of many colours.
Sunlight is only yellow.
options.why: The band showed many colours, from red to violet.

options.text: Glass makes its own light.
options.why: Glass is not a light source. It only bends light passing through it.

hints: A prism is a block of glass that bends light.
Newton also used a second prism to join the colours back together.
Ask where the colours must have come from if a prism can turn them back into white light.
items.explanation: The prism bent each colour by a different amount and spread them out. Because a second prism could join them back into white light, Newton showed that white light is a mixture of colours.

items.prompt: You see a rainbow in the late afternoon. Where must the Sun be?

options.text: in front of you, behind the rain
options.why: Rainbows are seen with the Sun behind you, shining onto raindrops in front of you.

options.text: directly above you
options.why: A rainbow cannot be seen when the Sun is very high in the sky.

options.text: behind you, shining on raindrops in front of you
hidden behind thick clouds
options.why: Sunlight must reach the raindrops for a rainbow to form.

hints: Raindrops split sunlight into colours and send some of it back towards you.
The light has to come from the Sun, hit the raindrops and then reach your eyes.
Picture the light coming back out of the raindrops. Decide where it must have come from.
items.explanation: Sunlight enters raindrops, is split into colours and reflects back out towards you. So the Sun must be behind you and the rain in front of you.

items.prompt: Label the diagram that shows how we see an object.

figure.alt: A bright round shape on the left, a square block in the middle and an eye shape on the right. Arrows join the bright shape to the block and the block to the eye.

hints: Tap a label, then tap its number.
The light source is the thing that makes light.
The arrows show light going from the source to the object and then on to the viewer.
items.explanation: The light source makes light. The light hits the object and bounces off it into the eye, and that is how we see the object.

items.prompt: A ray of light hits a flat mirror at 40° to the normal. Tap the ray that shows how it reflects.

figure.alt: A flat mirror lies along the bottom. A vertical line stands up from the mirror. A ray comes in from the upper left. Three rays labelled A, B and C leave the mirror to the right at different angles.

hints: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.
Both angles are measured from the normal, not from the mirror.
The reflected ray leaves the same angle away from the normal, on the other side.
items.explanation: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence. So the ray leaves at 40° to the normal, on the opposite side.

items.prompt: A ray of light hits a flat mirror and makes an angle of 30° with the surface of the mirror. What is the angle of incidence, measured from the normal?
hints: The normal is at right angles to the mirror.
A right angle is 90°.
Take the angle with the surface away from 90°.
items.explanation: The normal is 90° from the mirror surface. The angle from the normal is 90° − 30° = 60°.

items.caption: Letting light through
items.prompt: Complete the table. Choose from transparent, translucent or opaque.
head: Material
Light passes
Type
hints: Opaque materials block all the light.
Translucent materials let some light through but you cannot see clearly.
Look at the Light passes column for the missing rows.
items.explanation: Wood lets no light through, so it is opaque. Baking paper lets some light through, so it is translucent.

items.caption: Shadow of a stick on a clear day
items.prompt: Sekar measured the shadow of a 50 cm stick during the day. The Sun is at the same height before and after noon. Complete the table.
head: Time
Shadow (cm)
hints: Look for a pattern on either side of 12:00.
The Sun climbs until noon, then falls again.
14:00 is two hours after noon. Which time is two hours before noon?
items.explanation: The Sun is at the same height two hours after noon as two hours before. So 14:00 matches 10:00 and 16:00 matches 08:00.

items.prompt: Sort these into things that give out their own light and things that do not.
groups: Does not make its own light

items.text: a TV screen that is on

hints: A light source makes its own light.
The Moon is a tricky one.
The Moon shines because it reflects the light of something else.
items.explanation: The Sun, a flame, a firefly and a screen make light. The Moon, a mirror, a book and a wall only reflect light.

items.prompt: Sort these materials by how they let light through.
hints: Transparent: you can see clearly through.
Translucent: light comes through but the picture is blurry.
Opaque: no light comes through.
items.explanation: Transparent materials show clear pictures. Translucent ones scatter the light. Opaque ones block it.

items.prompt: Order the steps that let you see a ship over a wall using a periscope.
items: Light from the ship enters the top of the periscope
hints: Follow the light from the ship to your eye.
A periscope has a mirror at each end.
The top mirror is the first thing the light meets after entering.
items.explanation: Light enters at the top, reflects off the top mirror, goes down the tube, reflects off the bottom mirror and then enters the eye.

items.prompt: At midday the shadow of a flagpole is much shorter than at 8 o'clock in the morning. Why?

options.text: The Sun is higher in the sky at midday.
The Earth is closer to the Sun at midday.
options.why: Earth's distance from the Sun hardly changes during the day.

options.text: The flagpole becomes shorter in the heat.
options.why: The flagpole stays the same length.

options.text: The Sun gives out less light at midday.
options.why: The Sun's light output does not change. Its height in the sky does.

hints: Think about where the Sun is in the sky at different times.
A high light source makes a short shadow.
Compare the Sun at 8 o'clock and at midday.
items.explanation: At midday the Sun is high in the sky, so the shadow is short. In the morning the Sun is low, so the shadow is long.

items.prompt: Citra says: "We see things because our eyes send out light beams that touch objects." Which fact shows she is wrong?

options.text: We can see a bright lamp in the dark, even without a beam from our eyes.
We cannot see in the dark because our beams get tired.
options.why: That is not a fact. Eyes do not send out anything.

options.text: Light only travels in curved lines.
options.why: Light travels in straight lines.

options.text: Objects can only be seen when they are very close.
options.why: We can see a distant star.

hints: Which way does the light actually travel?
Think about what happens to our eyes in a completely dark room.
Light from a light source or reflected from an object has to enter the eye.
items.explanation: We see when light from a source, or light reflected from an object, enters our eyes. Eyes do not send out beams.

items.prompt: A black cat sits in a room that is completely dark, with the door shut. Can you see the cat?

options.text: Yes, because cats' eyes shine.
options.why: Eyes do not make light.

options.text: Yes, because black things give out their own light.
options.why: Black things absorb light and do not make any.

options.text: No, because black things cannot be seen.
options.why: Black things can be seen if there is light around them.

options.text: No, because there is no light to reflect off the cat into your eyes.

hints: To see something, light must reach your eyes.
Is there any light source in the room?
Think about what the cat can reflect.
items.explanation: With no light there is nothing to reflect off the cat and travel to your eyes, so you cannot see anything.

items.prompt: Joko holds a toy in front of a lamp so that it casts a shadow on a wall. He moves the toy closer to the lamp. What happens to the shadow?

options.text: It gets smaller.
options.why: A closer object blocks more of the light, making a bigger shadow.

options.text: It gets bigger.
It stays the same size.
options.why: The distance from the lamp changes the size of the shadow.

options.text: It disappears.
options.why: The toy still blocks the light.

hints: Light travels in straight lines.
A closer object blocks a wider fan of rays.
Picture the light rays spreading out from the lamp.
items.explanation: Light spreads out from the lamp. The closer the toy is to the lamp, the more rays it blocks, so the shadow on the wall is larger.

items.prompt: Choose all the surfaces that reflect light clearly enough to show a picture of your face.

options.text: a shiny spoon
a flat mirror
a rough stone
calm water in a bowl
black velvet cloth

hints: A clear picture needs a smooth, shiny surface.
Rough surfaces scatter the light in many directions.
Which three are smooth and shiny?
items.explanation: Smooth and shiny surfaces such as a mirror, a spoon and calm water reflect light in an ordered way. Rough stone and cloth scatter light.

items.prompt: When light changes direction as it passes from air into water, this is called ___.
hints: It is the reason a straw looks bent in a glass of water.
It happens when light changes speed.
The word starts with re and ends with tion.
items.explanation: The bending of light when it passes from one material into another is called refraction.

items.prompt: A red apple looks red because it reflects red light and ___ the other colours.
hints: Light that is not reflected goes somewhere.
The apple does not let the other colours through either.
The apple takes the other colours in. What is that called?
items.explanation: The apple reflects red light into our eyes and absorbs the other colours.

items.prompt: Light travels in ___ lines. When it bounces off a surface, this is called ___.
hints: Think about how light makes sharp shadows.
Refraction is a different word for bending.
A mirror makes light bounce back.
items.explanation: Light travels in straight lines. Reflection is when light bounces off a surface.

items.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: light bending as it enters a new material
light being taken in by a surface
the dark area where light is blocked
hints: Think about what each word looks like in a picture.
Refraction is the bending of light.
Shadows are made when light is blocked.
items.explanation: Reflection bounces light, refraction bends it, absorption takes it in and a shadow forms where light is blocked.

items.prompt: Amara measures the height of a shadow when a card is 20 cm from a lamp. She measures it once and writes 36 cm. What would make her result more reliable?

options.text: Measure the shadow again several times and find the mean.
Change the lamp to a brighter one.
options.why: Changing the lamp would change the test, not make the measurement more reliable.

options.text: Move the card closer to the lamp.
options.why: That changes the thing she is testing.

options.text: Only write down the biggest number.
options.why: A good scientist uses all the readings.

hints: A single reading might have a mistake.
How can you check that the same result happens every time?
Repeating the measurement and averaging reduces errors.
items.explanation: Repeating the measurement and finding the mean lowers the effect of mistakes, so the result is more reliable.

items.prompt: Kofi sees a flash of lightning. He hears the thunder 6 seconds later. Sound travels at 340 m/s. How far away was the lightning, in metres?
hints: Light reaches you almost instantly, so the 6 seconds is the time for the sound.
Use distance = speed × time.
Multiply 340 by 6.
items.explanation: The light arrives almost at once, so the 6 s is the travel time of the sound. 340 m/s × 6 s = 2040 m.

items.prompt: True or false: We see an object when light from it enters our eyes.

options.text: True
False

hints: Where does the light go?
Eyes receive light.
Light reaches the eye.
items.explanation: Light reflects off objects into our eyes, or comes from a source directly.

items.prompt: True or false: We see things because our eyes send out light.

options.text: True
False

hints: Do eyes glow?
What enters the eye?
Light enters eyes.
items.explanation: Eyes do not send out light. They only receive the light that comes from or is reflected off objects.

items.prompt: True or false: A mirror reflects light and the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

options.text: True
False

hints: Which angles match?
Light bounces.
They are equal.
items.explanation: Light bounces off at the same angle as it came in.

items.prompt: True or false: Refraction is when light bounces back off a mirror.

options.text: True
False

hints: Which word means bending?
A straw looks bent in water.
Refraction bends light.
items.explanation: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one material into another, such as from air into water. Bouncing is reflection.

items.prompt: Light bending as it enters water is called ___.
hints: A straw looks bent in water.
It starts with ref.
The word ends in tion.
items.explanation: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes into another material.
